name: Forensic Chemistry
tagline: Crime-scene analysis, toxicology, and evidence-based chemical identification.
seo_title: Forensic Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Forensic Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in forensic toxicology, drug analysis, trace evidence and fire debris analysis.

definition.lead: Forensic chemistry applies analytical chemistry to legal questions: what is this substance, where did it come from, and will the result stand up in court?
definition.body: It identifies drugs, poisons, fibres, paints and inks, and links traces to their sources. Every result must be reproducible, documented and defensible under cross-examination.

timeline.title: Toxicology is born
timeline.text: Mathieu Orfila publishes his treatise on poisons.
timeline.why: The first systematic approach to detecting poisons.

timeline.title: The Marsh test
timeline.text: James Marsh publishes a sensitive test for arsenic.
timeline.why: Arsenic, a common poison, became detectable.

timeline.title: The first police laboratory
timeline.text: Edmond Locard opens a forensic laboratory in Lyon.

timeline.title: The Breathalyzer
timeline.text: Robert Borkenstein invents a practical breath-alcohol instrument.

timeline.title: GC–MS
timeline.text: Roland Gohlke and Fred McLafferty couple gas chromatography to mass spectrometry.
timeline.why: Became the gold standard for identifying drugs and residues.

timeline.title: First DNA conviction
timeline.text: Colin Pitchfork is convicted in England using DNA evidence; DNA had also cleared an innocent suspect.
timeline.why: DNA can both convict and exonerate.

timeline.title: A call for rigour
timeline.text: The US National Academy of Sciences report 'Strengthening Forensic Science' is published.
timeline.why: Pushed for validation and standards across forensic methods.

quiz.explain: Arsenic is converted to arsine gas, which deposits a metallic film when heated.

quiz.q: What is the standard technique to confirm a seized drug?
quiz.explain: Separation plus a mass spectrum gives a near-certain identification.

options: A quick screening test that must be confirmed
Final proof accepted by any court
A DNA test carried out at the scene
A court ruling on the evidence
quiz.explain: Colour tests can give false positives.
Alcohol in breath is proportional to alcohol in blood.

options: A documented record of who handled evidence, and when
A list of suspects linked to the evidence
The laboratory equipment used for tests
A court order allowing evidence to be seized
quiz.explain: A broken chain can make evidence inadmissible.

quiz.q: Ignitable liquids in fire debris are identified by…
quiz.explain: Each fuel gives a characteristic pattern of peaks.

quiz.q: Why use infrared spectroscopy on paint chips?
options: It reveals the binder and pigment chemistry, so samples can be compared
It dates the car to the exact year it was made
It shows only the colour of the paint
It weighs the chip to identify its source
quiz.explain: Car paints have characteristic layered chemistry.

quiz.q: What did the 2009 US National Academy of Sciences report criticize?
options: The lack of scientific validation for several forensic methods
The uniforms worn by police officers
quiz.explain: It called for research, standards and independence.

quiz.q: Luminol glows on contact with traces of…
options: Blood, because haem catalyses its oxidation
Water, because it reacts with any liquid
quiz.explain: It is a presumptive test; other substances can also trigger it.
